Flickering candlelight, exceptional wine, and the quiet magic of the ranch in winter—Winterlight is back. @DrMohanYadav51 
●● "When a Nest Falls, Only the Bird Knows — Dr. Mohan Yadav’s Tear-Laden Eyes Roll with Hidden Agony" ●●
<*><*><*><*><*>
It is never easy to bring down the inheritance of a nest. Only the bird knows that ache in full. In Dr Mohan Yadav’s tears there was a letter no one had written—folded inside the eyes, addressed to a house that could no longer answer.

In Abdalpura, Ujjain, there stood a home his grandfather Ramchandra Yadav raised in 1974. In that courtyard a child was born. In those rooms he ran, fell, laughed, grew. For Simhastha 2028 a road had to widen. Nearly three metres of that house lay on the line. The Chief Minister did not send a file. He came himself. He offered prayer at the door. Then he lifted the pickaxe.

Power can order a wall to fall. It cannot order the heart to stay quiet. The man who governs a state stood for a moment as only a son. The throat tightened. The eyes filled. He said what every ordinary person already knows: the house where you were born, where you played, is not merely brick. To strike it is to strike a memory that still lives in the body.

This is the tenderness of the scene. Development has its arithmetic—pilgrims by the million, a city that must breathe, a festival that cannot wait. The sum is correct. Political power and Christianity don’t mix, we’ve been told. It is always and everywhere bad for Christians to wield civic authority.

Offered as perennial proof of this claim are the crusades and the Inquisition — which, admittedly, were not Christianity’s finest hour.

But what if those events, which happened hundreds and even a thousand years ago, were the exception that highlights the rule?

The church has been discipled by a secular (and increasingly Marxist) culture to believe that power is inherently a bad thing — something always to be challenged, even torn down.

This belief has caused Christians to retreat into their private lives and give up all ambition for worldly power.

In the intervening decades, guess who’s been very happy to fill the positions of power that Christians have vacated? Yes, the same secularists that told us that power is a bad thing.

It’s a clever play — and it’s time we stopped falling for it.

At least partly to blame for the church’s aversion to bold civic engagement is what Dr Michael Clary calls ‘loser theology’.

Dr Clary is the Lead Pastor at Christ the King Church in Cincinnati, Ohio in the United States, and has spent several years dissecting this phenomenon. He explains:

"At its core, loser theology convinces believers that asserting agency for Christ is inherently wrong. It frames passivity, weakness, and vague trust in God as the hallmarks of true faithfulness, while strength, conviction, and action are branded as dangerous forms of legalism and pride."

Clary adds that loser theology “offers a spiritualised excuse for being ineffective, weak, and lazy”.

It’s important to point out that loser theology isn’t explicitly taught in our churches. To quote the classic Australian film The Castle, it’s “the vibe of the thing”. Loser theology is more or less unspoken and absorbed passively, like the air we breathe.

Also, loser theology isn’t unique to theologically compromised churches. It’s very possible to hold fast to many solid biblical values and still cling to loser theology.

Here’s an example of how it works: Abortion is bad, but if Christians try to outlaw abortion, it would require us to seek political power. And since political power isn’t “the way of Jesus”, it’s better that we just pray and trust God instead.

Do you see it?

“Loser theology is attractive because it replaces biblical virtues with pseudo-virtues,” Dr Clary goes on to explain. “Powerlessness, poverty, weakness [and] insecurity are elevated as true marks of holiness.”

He adds that loser theology locks us “in a state of permanent ineffectiveness while cloaking that failure in a false sense of moral superiority”.

The result is that Christians are rendered “impotent for doing anything beyond the realm of their private devotional lives”.

The Bible verse most often used to justify loser theology is when Jesus Christ told Pilate, “my kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36).

Yes, God’s kingdom is not of this world — but that doesn’t mean God doesn’t want His kingdom to influence this world for the better.

The Bible is full of examples of godly people being raised up to serve in positions of political power to glorify God and bring about His purposes — whether Moses, Joseph, Daniel, Esther, Mordecai, Nehemiah, John the Baptist, Cornelius, or countless others.

Old Testament kings were commanded to keep their own copy of God’s law and live by it. Gentile rulers were commanded to bow the knee to Yahweh — like the king of Nineveh, who led his whole city to repent; or Nebuchadnezzar, who humbled himself and acknowledged that the Most High rules over the kingdoms of men; or Cyrus, who freed the Jewish exiles and sent them back to rebuild Jerusalem.

Even in the New Testament, we see Paul traversing Europe with a fire in his heart to preach the gospel to local rulers and even Caesar himself.

Scripture overflows with accounts of God’s people stepping boldly into roles of civic authority, or calling the rulers of this age to govern with righteousness.

In short, as Christians, we must overcome our addiction to “loser theology”.

No, we should not want power for power’s sake, or seek to build our own kingdoms, or conflate God’s kingdom with the kingdoms of this world, or fear that God’s purposes will somehow fail without our help.

But yes, we should long, pray and vote to see godly believers occupy positions of worldly authority.

Because it is good for Christians to wield political power.

8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An NPR reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook

text:
If you only care (understandably) about what @nejatian said during the $OPEN Army space yesterday, here it is below! 

Lots of great little nuggets here.

1. Jeff: Why only ~400 contracts a week? What’s the unlock to 5x? Top-of-funnel / more offers?
Kaz: Not mainly a top-of-funnel problem in core markets. OpenDoor has already said that in those markets, about 1 in 4 people who sell a home try OpenDoor at some point. That “native intent” is why he cut marketing by roughly an order of magnitude and growth still went up.
The constraint is offer relevancy. Old OpenDoor had one product: cash, sell fast, leave. Cash Now / More Later is now a family of products you tune to the seller. Relevancy is as hard as feed ranking on X or Instagram.
YoY improvement has mostly been better relevancy. That gets them a long way, not necessarily 5x. This year’s work is building the muscle for a strong next year — they haven’t been secretive about that.

2. Coronado loan originator: Shopify × Muse-style connector? People already asking ChatGPT for home values.
Kaz: There is already a working Muse connector prototype on his phone. Launching a connector is easy. Making it not a party trick is hard.
He used Meta as the cautionary tale: every bank shipped a Messenger product; almost all were unused. A demo that works in a narrow box is not a product.
They have the connector. He and Morgan had talked about it that same day. They will ship something only when it’s actually good.

3. Same originator: Can loan officers / LOS partners refer into OpenDoor?
Kaz: Yes in principle, not this year.
When he arrived, product/engineering had been gutted; prioritization has been painful. They finally have a realtor product he wouldn’t be embarrassed to use as an agent. They want that to hill-climb before adding more channels.
North star is Shopify-like infrastructure: live inside other people’s workflows, even if the customer never uses “all of OpenDoor.” It’s already in https://t.co/DhpSO6bdCN and https://t.co/RHXtDAsBz2, and he likes those experiences. Ideal end state: request and close an OpenDoor offer from inside the originator’s LOS.

4. Someone: 3P + tokenization — timing, in-house vs partners (tZERO / Figure)?
Kaz on 3P: Won’t discuss it. They’re actively working on several ideas. That is not an imminent-launch hint.
Kaz on tokenization: Tokenizing a house (LLC → tokens) is not the hard part; lots of people can do that.
The version he cares about is access: people who can’t get a mortgage yet buy a small slice (e.g. 1%), then climb toward the ~10% / credit / DTI they need. That matches the mission, cuts transaction friction, and avoids clunky secondary-market plumbing. Other structures are possible; that’s the one in his head.
They know the direction and have prototyped it. They haven’t shipped because they’re still fixing a large chunk of the company for next year. When they’re ready they’ll move fast. The market will need education so “own 1% of a house” doesn’t read as another me-too RWA toy.
Build vs partner: Write a line of code once. Partner when the other company is mission-aligned; build if not. He’s not jealous of someone else’s margin. Grow the pie first.

text:
Ultraprocessed Foods, Processed Meats, and Cognitive Decline

Tuesday, September 29, 2026
Dr. Joel P. Rutkowski

Medical Disclaimer:

The information presented in this paper is for informational, educational, and research purposes only and does not constitute formal medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. The clinical protocols, dietary recommendations, and herbal interventions discussed herein should not replace professional medical consultation, evaluation, or individualized care. Readers and patients should consult a qualified physician or licensed healthcare provider before making major dietary alterations, eliminating medical therapies, or initiating new herbal and supplement regimens, particularly if managing pre-existing health conditions or taking prescription medications.

Abstract

Recent epidemiological and translational milestones—epitomized by the landmark 2026 synthesis by Carmichael and colleagues published in the Annual Review of Nutrition—have drawn intense scientific and public scrutiny to the nexus between ultraprocessed foods (UPFs) and neurodegenerative aging. Synthesizing data spanning nearly a century of nutritional science (1940–2026), this review evaluates the epidemiological link demonstrating a 44 to 52 percent increased risk of dementia associated with an incremental intake of 25 grams (g)/day of processed meat. We examine the mechanistic underpinnings—focusing on systemic inflammation, blood-brain barrier degradation, and nitrosamine neurotoxicity—and establish an exhaustive, actionable clinical protocol built on dietary displacement, the MIND-Mediterranean framework, cognitive stress hygiene, traditional healing modalities (Traditional Chinese Medicine and Ayurveda), targeted medicinal herbs, and microgreen-derived bioactive compounds.

1. Comprehensive Literature Review (1940–2026)

The scientific discourse on diet and cognitive health has undergone three distinct evolutionary epochs over the past eight decades.

During the first phase spanning the 1940s through the 1970s, post-World War II nutritional science prioritized the eradication of overt deficiency diseases, such as niacin deficiency-induced pellagra dementia and thiamine-deficiency Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Food was evaluated strictly through its reductionist components, including vitamins, essential amino acids, and basic macros. Chronic non-communicable neurodegenerative diseases were viewed primarily as unmodifiable genetic outcomes or inevitable consequences of aging.

The second phase, covering the 1980s through the 2010s, marked the vascular and dietary pattern revolution. As life expectancies rose, epidemiological cohorts like the Framingham Heart Study and the Lyon Diet Heart Study shifted focus toward chronic disease prevention. Researchers identified that midlife vascular risk factors strongly predicted late-life dementia. This era established the Mediterranean Diet and the MIND diet, proving that whole food matrices rich in polyphenols and unsaturated fats protect cognitive integrity. Conversely, early warnings regarding saturated fats and preserved meats emerged, though they were often overshadowed by total-fat reduction dogmas.

The current phase, spanning from 2020 to 2026, represents the ultraprocessed food and neuro-inflammatory paradigm. The formalization of the NOVA food classification system revolutionized nutritional epidemiology by categorizing foods by the extent and purpose of industrial processing rather than mere nutrient content. Landmark studies, including the multi-institutional synthesis across 26 institutions and over 500,000 participants led by Dr. Owen Carmichael at Pennington Biomedical Research Center, have directly implicated UPFs and processed meats in accelerating biological brain aging. These findings link every 25g daily increment of processed meat to a 44 to 52 percent elevation in dementia risk, demonstrating neurocognitive damage via gut-brain axis disruption, microglial priming, and cerebral microvascular degeneration.

2. Mechanistic Pathways: How Processed Meats Harm the Brain

The biological mechanisms driving processed meat-induced cognitive decline are multifactorial and interconnected.

Chemical preservatives like sodium nitrate and nitrite interact with amines during processing and high-heat cooking, forming carcinogenic and neurotoxic N-nitroso compounds. These compounds induce oxidative stress and DNA damage in neural tissues. Simultaneously, systemic low-grade inflammation triggered by high-sodium, high-fat, and additive-laden UPFs degrades endothelial tight junctions in cerebral microvessels. This degradation allows circulating cytokines and peripheral toxins to infiltrate the brain parenchyma. Furthermore, industrial emulsifiers, artificial colorings, and a lack of dietary fiber alter the gut microbiome, driving an increase in lipopolysaccharides that activate brain microglia, leading to chronic neuroinflammation and synaptic pruning in the memory-processing centers of the hippocampus.

3. Best Strategic Framework to Manage and Stop Cognitive Decline

Mitigating the neurodegenerative risks posed by modern dietary environments requires a multi-layered, actionable framework built on five core pillars.

The first strategy is dietary displacement. Individuals should aim to replace 10 percent of daily ultraprocessed food and processed meat calories with unprocessed whole foods, a shift supported by mathematical modeling showing a corresponding 19 percent reduction in dementia risk.

The second strategy involves adopting the MIND and Mediterranean dietary matrices, which prioritize leafy greens, berries, nuts, beans, and fatty fish to deliver high concentrations of neuroprotective antioxidants and omega-3s that stabilize cell membranes.

The third strategy focuses on the thought diet and cognitive resilience. Implementing mindfulness, cognitive reserve building, and stress-reduction protocols lowers cortisol, which otherwise synergizes with systemic inflammation to exacerbate hippocampal atrophy.

The fourth strategy incorporates traditional healing philosophies, specifically Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) and Ayurveda, to address root systemic imbalances, clear metabolic toxins, and restore vitality to the brain-body axis.

The fifth strategy centers on phytochemical and microgreen augmentation. Integrating targeted herbs and nutrient-dense microgreens daily delivers high-potency polyphenols and sulforaphane capable of crossing the blood-brain barrier to neutralize reactive oxygen species.

4. Therapeutic Modalities: Thought Diet, Traditional Medicine, Herbs, and Microgreens

The Thought Diet

Just as the physical diet feeds the gut-brain axis, the thought diet regulates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Chronic psychological stress and cognitive stagnation elevate systemic cortisol and pro-inflammatory cytokines, which accelerate neurodegeneration. Daily cognitive stimulation involving novel learning and complex problem-solving, combined with mindfulness-based stress reduction, upregulates brain-derived neurotrophic factor to counteract neuro-synaptic damage.

Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) Perspectives

In TCM, cognitive decline and memory fading are understood through imbalances such as Kidney Essence deficiency, Spleen Qi deficiency leading to dampness and phlegm accumulation, and Blood stasis blocking cerebral collaterals. Therapeutic approaches focus on tonifying Kidney Jing, resolving phlegm that mist the orifices of the mind, and invigorating microcirculatory flow. Key botanicals include Ginkgo biloba (Yin Xing Ye) to enhance cerebral microcirculation and Panax ginseng or Codonopsis to fortify Spleen Qi and mental clarity.

Ayurvedic Medicine Perspectives

Ayurveda frames neurodegeneration within disorders of memory loss driven by aggravated Vata dosha—bringing dryness, instability, and degeneration—alongside accumulated metabolic toxins known as Ama that block deep neurological micro-channels. Treatment strategies emphasize grounding, nourishing Rasayanas (rejuvenatives) that pacify Vata and nourish Majja dhatu (nervous tissue). Key botanicals include Bacopa monnieri (Brahmi) as a premier nootropic herb to sharpen intellect and Ashwagandha as a powerful adaptogen that lowers cortisol and shields neural networks from oxidative deterioration.

Neuroprotective Phytochemicals and Herbs

Phytochemical-rich herbs act as natural anti-inflammatory and anti-amyloidogenic agents. Rosemary contains rosmarinic and carnosic acids that inhibit acetylcholinesterase breakdown and scavenge free radicals within neural tissue. Curcumin from turmeric crosses the blood-brain barrier to bind plaques, suppress neuroinflammation, and stimulate neurogenesis in the hippocampus.

The Power of Microgreens

Microgreens, which are cotyledon-stage greens such as broccoli, red cabbage, and radish, represent a potent nutritional countermeasure against UPF-induced oxidative stress. Broccoli microgreens contain up to 40 times higher concentrations of vital phytonutrients like glucoraphanin—the precursor to sulforaphane—than mature plants. Sulforaphane activates the Nrf2 pathway, ramping up the brain's internal antioxidant defense system and clearing cellular debris. Additionally, the high concentration of vitamin E, carotenoids, and polyphenols in microgreens supports endothelial health, preserving the structural integrity of the blood-brain barrier against microvascular insults.

5. Clinical Protocol and Actionable Implementation

To translate this 1940–2026 evidence base into clinical practice, the single most effective starting point is the 10 percent Ultraprocessed Food (UPF) Swap paired with daily microgreen integration and holistic herbal routines. This intervention optimizes vascular integrity and engages cellular defense mechanisms immediately.

Step-by-Step Daily Execution Plan

    • Step 1: Complete Elimination of Processed Meats
      
        ◦ Action: Immediately remove pre-packaged deli meats, hot dogs, bacon, and cured sausages from the diet.
          
        ◦ Alternative: Substitute with clean, whole-protein sources such as wild-caught salmon, pasture-raised eggs, organic chicken breast, or smashed chickpeas with extra virgin olive oil and fresh herbs.
          
    • Step 2: The 10 Percent Caloric Displacement Swap
      
        ◦ Action: Identify common convenience snacks or processed items (such as packaged crackers, sugary yogurts, or processed snack bars) and replace them with whole-food alternatives like raw walnuts, almonds, or fresh berries.
          
    • Step 3: Daily Microgreen Integration
      
        ◦ Action: Consume one-quarter cup of fresh broccoli or red cabbage microgreens daily. Incorporate them into salads, wraps, or grain bowls to deliver high concentrations of glucoraphanin for Nrf2-mediated cellular detoxification.
          
    • Step 4: Herbal, TCM, and Ayurvedic Routine Synergy
      
        ◦ Action: Supplement daily meals with therapeutic and adaptogenic herbs like Brahmi (Bacopa), Ashwagandha, turmeric, and rosemary, while dedicating 5 to 10 minutes to mindfulness deep-breathing or novel cognitive tasks to suppress cortisol and elevate brain-derived neurotrophic factor.
          
6. Conclusion, Comprehensive Discussion, and Final Thoughts

The convergence of historical nutritional epidemiology, modern neuro-inflammatory science, and ancient medical philosophies establishes a paradigm-shifting understanding of brain aging. For decades, modern medicine treated cognitive decline as an inevitable consequence of genetic predisposition or chronological aging, focusing largely on late-stage symptom management or narrow nutritional deficiencies. 

However, the landmark 2026 synthesis by Carmichael and colleagues, alongside decades of accumulating data on the NOVA food classification system, shatters this deterministic view. We now recognize that the modern industrial food environment—heavily saturated with ultraprocessed foods (UPFs) and chemically preserved meats—is a primary external driver of accelerated neurodegeneration, microvascular degradation, and cognitive erosion.

The data linking a 44 to 52 percent increased dementia risk to a modest 25 grams daily increment of processed meat demands an urgent re-evaluation of public health priorities and clinical practice. The mechanistic reality is clear: nitrosamine neurotoxicity, blood-brain barrier breakdown, gut dysbiosis, and chronic microglial activation create a destructive cascade that literally alters brain architecture. Stopping and reversing this trajectory requires moving beyond reductionist diets toward multi-layered, synergistic interventions.

Integrating modern phytochemical science with the wisdom of Traditional Chinese Medicine and Ayurveda bridges a critical gap in contemporary healthcare. While modern science identifies the molecular pathways of sulforaphane, curcumin, and rosmarinic acid, ancient healing traditions provide a holistic framework for managing the systemic foundations of vitality. TCM insights into Kidney Essence (Jing) preservation and Spleen Qi support, combined with Ayurvedic principles of pacifying Vata and clearing metabolic toxins (Ama), offer profound clinical value. They remind us that preserving cognition is not merely about blocking an inflammatory enzyme or shielding a cellular membrane; it is about restoring systemic harmony across the gut-brain-mind axis.

Ultimately, protecting cognitive longevity is an active, daily practice. By implementing structured dietary displacement, adopting whole-food MIND-Mediterranean matrices, practicing cognitive stress hygiene, utilizing targeted traditional botanicals, and incorporating nutrient-dense microgreens, clinicians and patients possess an empowering roadmap. The transition away from ultraprocessed toxins toward a biologically coherent lifestyle is not just a strategy for preventing dementia—it is an investment in sustained human agency, mental clarity, and long-term vitality.

text:
MISPERCIEVED "GUILT BY ASSOCIATION" IS A NON-SEQUITUR FALLACY, THUS FAILS TO ESTABLISH PROOF AGAINST PAULINE HANSON.

For example: if I lived in America and made a comment about you, we'd be framed by those who share the same illogical thinking structure as 'best buddies' even though we're complete strangers? 🤭

COULD CHANNEL 9 HAVE HEAD-SHRUNK YOU BY WEAPONIZED PSYCHOLOGY?

Lets explore this idea, shall we?

1  ADJACENCY AND FRAMING.

If footage of extremists, narration about white supremacy and images of Hanson are placed in sequence, viewers may infer a relationship stronger than the stated facts.

That is a plausible editorial-effect concern, not proof that Nine intended viewers to equate them.

The reported narration makes the distinction between “extreme corners” and “the mainstream”, but the transition itself still merits inspection.

2 ASSOCIATIVE CONTAMINATION

Robb’s Klan identity is highly salient.

Viewers may carry the emotional force of that identity over to the person he praises, rather than ask precisely what proposition his praise proves.

Research on ILLUSORY CORRELATION shows how distinctive pairings can produce or exaggerate perceived associations; a laboratory finding does not, however, measure the effect of this particular broadcast.

3 THE INTERVIEWER’S CUE

“Heartening” supplied an evaluative frame in the filmed question, which Robb accepted with “encouraging”.

That warrants criticism of the question’s construction.

It does not negate his earlier reported remarks about Hanson or show that Nine introduced her name in the off-camera conversation.

4 PRIOR COMMITMENTS

A viewer already convinced Hanson is extremist may treat Robb’s praise as conclusive

A supporter already convinced Nine is hostile may treat the same exchange as proof of a setup.

CONFIRMATION BIAS and IDENTITY-PROTECTIVE COGNITION offers plausible explanations for both reactions, but is a diagnoses only individual viewers may conduct on themselves however will only serve them well if done with genuine honest concern driven curiosity (as I did to myself 20 years ago).

5 AUTHOR-ITY -> RESPONSIBILITY -> ACCOUNTABILITY

A broadcaster can be responsible for a foreseeably misleading implication even if no manager intended to mislead anyone.

Why ask a Klan leader whether Hanson’s success was “heartening”, and what did the team expect viewers to infer from the answer?

This gives the segment a potential two-directionpolarising effect:
-some opponents of One Nation may feel vindicated ();
-some supporters may feel unfairly accused and become more committed.

Experimental research finds that certain reports emphasising societal division can increase perceived polarisation and, through that pathway, hostility toward political opponents.

The researchers also stress that media effects are complex: their results support a risk mechanism, not an absolute causal finding. Audiences have to examine the impact upon themselves based on their preconceived positions.

Nine’s "public relations" position is that Robb introduced Hanson during interview preparation and that his comments were included to examine racial and political divisions.

That explains its stated rationale, but does not fully answer the question about the finished framing.

The logically sound formulation is: a foreseeable risk of an unsupported association called for an editorial safeguard.

That safeguard might have been explicit narration distinguishing Robb’s approval from Hanson’s beliefs, sufficient context around both positions, or a promotional cut that did not invite a stronger inference than the episode could substantiate.

Whether Nine provided adequate safeguards requires comparison of the complete broadcast with the shorter material as actually aired and circulated.

GEOPOLITICAL OVERREACH?

One Nation is an Australian party.
The documentary is about AMERICA’s political polarization.

On that stated remit, its inclusion needs an explanation of what it tells the viewer about America, rather than merely about Australian politics.

One Nation itself records that Hanson spoke at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago in Florida.

Also, an American interview subject bringing up an Australian politician can be evidence of how that American subject interprets political developments abroad.

Neither fact makes One Nation an American political party, nor establishes that it influenced US voters or the midterms.

The Mar-a-Lago appearance should not be conflated with a verified personal meeting or particular discourse with Trump; the source establishes the speech at his resort, not those further details.

The missing premise is a demonstrated bridge between the Australian example (Pauline Hanson & One Nation) and the American subject.

The argument would need to look something like this:

1 Robb’s views are relevant to the documentary’s examination of divisions in the US.

2 His reference to Hanson reveals something materially relevant about those US divisions.

3 The edit makes clear that it is presenting Robb’s perception, not evidence about One Nation’s ideology or role in America.

Premise 1 is straightforward.
Premise 2 is plausible but requires an editorial explanation;
Premise 3 depends on the finished sequence.

Without them, the audience may be misled from “an American extremist praised an Australian politician” to “that politician belongs in the same political category”.

That is a non sequitur fallacy, not a conclusion supplied by geography, a shared immigration topic, or Robb’s approval alone.

THE QUESTIONS I WOULD PUT TO CHANNEL NINE ARE THEREFORE:

1 Who approved the question about whether Hanson’s success was “heartening”, and on what editorial rationale?

2 What did the team know of Robb’s remarks before filming, and what recording or notes support the account that he first mentioned Hanson unprompted?

3 How did the edit distinguish “Robb praises Hanson” from “Hanson shares Robb’s ideology”?

4 Who reviewed the broadcast segment and each promotion for that foreseeable inference?

5 What evidence, if any, supports a claim that the broadcast increased polarisation beyond the observable backlash and follow-up coverage?

6. At a time when One Nation was a live Australian electoral contender, what Australian inference would an ordinary viewer be invited to draw from placing its leader beside a Klan figure in a series titled “The Divided States” - and what did Nine do to prevent an unsupported inference?

Channel Nine should be asked to account for professional judgment and foreseeable consequences.

It does not give the corporation an innocence-by-default pass simply because its private intentions are inaccessible; nor does it turn foreseeable harm into proof of a deliberate plan.

THE IRONIC IMBALANCE BETWEEN PUBLIC DISCOURSE AND MEDIA INTEGRITY

The public (as constituents) are increasingly subject to restrictions and moderation when speaking online, yet professionally produced political media may still shape opinion through implications that are harder to test than explicit factual errors.

Nine’s Robb–Hanson sequence should be assessed not only for whether the quotations were accurate, but for whether its framing supported the inference it invited Australian viewers to draw.

JOHN KIRIAKOU: THE FBI FOUND A LONELY HOMELESS MAN, AND BUILT A TERROR CASE 

Harun Abdul-Malik Yener was a homeless 30-year-old in Florida with no money, no travel plans, and no support system.

According to the defense, the FBI entered his life posing as members of an anti-government militia. They offered friendship, support, and a sense of belonging.

Then came the plot: targeting the New York Stock Exchange. Investigators introduced the idea and promised help obtaining explosives.

Yener’s most advanced weapon was reportedly a used pressure cooker from a pawn shop. Yet the government presented his arrest as the disruption of a major terror plot.

Yener had no independent means to carry out an attack, and no allies beyond the people he believed supported him. On June 30, 2026, a Miami jury acquitted him on all charges.

The case raises a serious question: how many isolated, poor, or mentally unwell young men are drawn into FBI operations by people offering them friendship and purpose, then guided toward plans they could not carry out alone?

That is not simply stopping crime. It is creating the conditions for it. @JohnKiriakou served as an expert witness for Yener’s defense and shares the story behind the case.

Old Flame (Gambler's Folly Book 4) by Mellie Miller is a heartfelt second-chance paranormal shifter romance that blends emotional healing, mature love, and the magic of fate. Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. A slow-burn friends-to-lovers tale full of heart, sensuality, and the series’ signature fantasy charm.

About the author
Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. Married to her one and only, Steve, they began their journey through life in 1976 and, after two children and many moves, she finally has the time to devote to this love. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. She and her husband live in rural Georgia and share their lives with cats, dogs, and a flock of chickens. She also writes under the pen name Sultonna Nadine.

text:
Samsung's 2nm Foundry Yield Reportedly Nears 60% as It Goes All Out on Power Efficiency

Samsung Electronics' Foundry Business has reportedly raised the yield of its 2nm (SF2) process to close to 60% as it targets orders from big tech customers. Having moved past the yield stabilization phase, Samsung is said to be focusing its engineering resources on technical maturity, including performance per watt, through discussions with prospective customers. The company is determined to use next year's 2nm chip supply to Tesla as a springboard for winning more big tech customers in earnest.

2nm Yield Nears 60%, but Performance per Watt Is the Key

According to industry sources on the 29th, Samsung's SF2 yield has improved from the mid 50% range the market had previously estimated and has reportedly now reached around 60%. The market had estimated that yield, which was in the 30% range in mid last year, rose to the 50% range in January this year and to around 55% in August.

SF2 is Samsung's first generation 2nm process built on a gate all around (GAA) structure. Its first mass production product is Samsung's own mobile application processor (AP), the Exynos 2600. The Exynos 2600 is produced on the S3 line in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province, and went into some Galaxy S26 series models earlier this year. For this chip, Samsung used a package structure that places a copper Heat Path Block (HPB) on top of the memory, which improved thermal resistance by 30%.

After launch, however, some overseas tests found that the Exynos 2600 used more power than Qualcomm's latest Snapdragon on the same workload, which drew criticism of its power efficiency. Some also saw this as a limitation of the process itself. To address this, Samsung is preparing its second generation 2nm process, SF2P, with mass production targeted for this year. Compared with SF2, SF2P reportedly delivers 12% higher performance, 25% lower power consumption and 8% smaller chip area.

With yield now on track, Samsung is said to be focusing on performance stability at the mass production stage. The company has reportedly put a large share of its engineering staff on making sure performance per watt, including heat and power consumption, does not vary once its chips are built into customer products. This is expected to support its case for technical reliability in future negotiations with large fabless (chip design) customers.

TSMC Alone at the Top, Samsung and Intel Fighting for Second

Intel, Samsung's competitor, is mass producing Panther Lake on its 2nm class 18A process at Fab 52 in Arizona. It is viewed as having achieved some success within its own product lineup, including a 56% share of the artificial intelligence (AI) PC market. However, 18A has yet to win any notable external foundry customers, and there is reportedly a view within Intel that it must stake its bid for external customers on the next generation 14A process (targeting mass production in 2027 or later).

TSMC is a step ahead of both companies after securing orders from big tech companies such as Apple. By absorbing existing customers such as Apple, AMD and Nvidia wholesale, it recorded a 72.5% share of the foundry (contract chip manufacturing) market as of Q2 this year, which widened its lead over Samsung Foundry (5.9%). 2nm wafer prices have settled at around $30,000, 50% higher than 3nm ($20,000), and TSMC has kept a "no discount" policy that offers no separate discounts even to large customers. The industry believes TSMC's 2nm capacity (CAPA) is booked through 2028.

As a result, observers expect a structure in which Samsung and Intel compete for second place behind a dominant TSMC. The prevailing view is that the timing of Samsung Foundry's return to profitability is tied to utilization at its Taylor fab. A semiconductor industry official said, "Yield approaching 60% and the start of work on improving performance per watt are meaningful signs of a rebound," but added, "The share gap with TSMC is so wide that it will take more time before this leads to any real change in the market structure."

text:
Rebuilding SmackDown: A Return to Wrestling Television

SmackDown should distinguish itself from Raw through competitive wrestling, technical variety, emerging talent, meaningful championships and a gritty sports-oriented presentation. Rather than copying the Ruthless Aggression Era, it should modernize the philosophy that made the brand feel unique.

Its roster already supports this identity. Gunther, Sami Zayn, CM Punk, Kevin Owens, Finn Bálor, Randy Orton, Johnny Gargano, Rey Fenix, Shinsuke Nakamura and Trick Williams offer contrasting styles, while Giulia, Charlotte Flair, Tiffany Stratton, Jade Cargill, Jacy Jayne and Lash Legend could anchor an equally competitive women’s division.

SmackDown would feature three brand-exclusive championships: the United States Championship, Women’s United States Championship and Cruiserweight Championship. The United States titles would serve as workhorse championships, rewarding consistent performances and credible victories. The Cruiserweight Championship would spotlight speed, technical wrestling and high-flying ability. Rankings, tournaments, open challenges, time limits and best-of-seven series would give each title a clear competitive purpose.

The show could draw from classic SmackDown formulas: open challenges that introduce new talent, elite wrestling rivalries, competitive friendships, Iron Man matches, steel cages and occasional chaotic stipulations. Realism would come through selective records, injury updates, meaningful losses and commentary focused on strategy, conditioning and technique. Wrestlers would have identifiable strengths and weaknesses, and victories would determine future opportunities.

This would create a clear contrast with Raw. Raw could remain WWE’s larger, spectacle-driven program, while SmackDown becomes the place where wrestlers prove themselves. Raw asks, “What will happen?” SmackDown asks, “Who will win?”

The presentation should reinforce that identity through a grainy, standard-definition-inspired aesthetic: softer images, film grain, darker lighting, handheld ringside cameras, restrained graphics and occasional 4:3-style video packages. A blue, industrial visual design and minimalist statistics would make the show immediately recognizable.

With its exclusive championships, competitive structure and distinctive presentation, SmackDown could become WWE’s dedicated home for athleticism, realism and wrestling.

OGUN STATE SEAPORT DP WORLD

On 24 September 2026, in Paris, the Ogun State Government and DP World signed Memoranda of Understanding to build the Gateway Deep Sea Port and the Ogun State Blue Marine Special Economic Zone, witnessed by President Bola Tinubu. The numbers are substantial: an initial investment exceeding $7 billion, a four-kilometre berth with an 18-metre natural draft deep enough for Post-Panamax vessels, and a Special Economic Zone spanning 10,000 hectares. 

OBIDENTS PROPAGANDA 
Within hours, a segment of online commentary, spearheaded by vocal elite commentators from the South East, had recast a commercial agreement as fresh proof that President Tinubu is “Yorubanising” Nigeria’s maritime infrastructure. It is a serious charge dressed in urgent language, and it deserves a serious answer, not a shrug.

FACTS FROM LIES AND MYTH

The answer begins with what a Memorandum of Understanding actually is. This was not a federal loan, and no state debt was created. It is a Public-Private Partnership in which DP World and its financial partners will deploy their own equity and raise private capital to construct and operate the port, while Ogun State’s contribution is land, right-of-way facilitation and the regulatory framework for the Special Economic Zone. 

Federal Government Role
The Federal Government’s role, by its own account, is confined to regulatory clarity and matching infrastructure such as road and rail links, not to underwriting anyone’s risk. Put simply, DP World is not extracting from Nigeria; DP World is the one bringing the money, because Ogun Waterside offers what its money needs: an 18-metre draft that avoids the crushing dredging bills already draining Lagos, a direct link via the 28-kilometre Ogun stretch of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, and proximity to a manufacturing base that can turn imported raw materials into exports without ever leaving the same economic corridor.

text:
Approval for Modernisation and Upgrade of Onne, Rivers, Delta, Calabar Ports 

I am pleased to announce that the Federal Government has approved the comprehensive modernisation and upgrade of Onne, Rivers, Delta and Calabar Ports.

This approval builds on the earlier approval for the modernisation and upgrade of Apapa and Tin Can Island Ports in Lagos, reaffirming our determination to develop a balanced, efficient and globally competitive national port system.

Under the leadership of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu @officialABAT, infrastructure renewal and economic diversification remain central to the Renewed Hope Agenda. Modern and efficient ports are critical to this vision because they facilitate trade, support industry, attract investment and create jobs.

Extending the modernisation programme beyond Lagos will complement ongoing investments in Apapa and Tin Can Island, while helping to reduce the concentration of cargo traffic around Lagos and creating additional efficient gateways for international trade.

Upgraded infrastructure and improved operational efficiency at Onne, Rivers, Delta and Calabar Ports will enhance cargo handling, reduce vessel turnaround times, strengthen regional connectivity and make the movement of goods more predictable and cost-effective.

These ports have strategic roles to play in our trade, industrial and regional development, and we are determined to equip them to meet the demands of a growing economy.

This is part of a broader expansion of Nigeria’s maritime infrastructure, including Federal Government approvals for the development of the Ibom, Bakassi, Agge, Gateway, Ondo and Bonny Deep Seaports.

Our approach is comprehensive. We are modernising existing ports while facilitating the development of new deep seaports. Together, these investments will expand Nigeria’s maritime capacity, create stronger economic corridors and position our country as a major maritime and logistics hub in Africa.

Our vision is an integrated maritime and logistics system in which ports, roads, rail, inland waterways and other transport infrastructure work together to enable the seamless movement of cargo.

We want Nigerian businesses to spend less time and resources moving their goods, while creating an environment that encourages investment and supports job creation.

The Ministry will continue to work closely with state governments, terminal operators, investors, shipping companies and other stakeholders to ensure that these projects translate into tangible improvements across Nigeria’s marine and blue economy.

Nigeria has the geography, market and maritime resources to become a leading maritime hub. Our responsibility is to provide the infrastructure, policies and enabling environment required to turn that potential into sustainable economic value.

The most absurd regulatory moment of my career was in late 2009/2010 being questioned on $CZR CDS trades leading up to the 2006 LBO.  When the sponsor deal was announced, the CDS widened to a [jaw dropping] rate or 250 bps.  Before the deal leaked it was 80 bps but widened to 112 when deal rumors started coming out.  Mind you,  Vegas at this point in time was nuts; a million casino and condo projects in process.  

Sitting there for these questions in the post GFC world where $CZR 5 year CDS was trading 15-20 pts upfront and 500 bps running was too insane for the lawyers to understand.  They kept asking what we knew and if the LBO was leaked…maybe 112 bps for levered casino CDS in 2006 was just the wrong price?  Even if a “strategic” was the winner.  Maybe, Vegas was about to be overbuilt and all the casinos were about to be toast?  One of the reasons so few people went to jail after the GFC was 💩 like this…the world almost ended and this lawyer wanted to understand why CDS went from 112 to 250 bps in 2006…that was literally the extent of their regulatory interest.  

$AIG was probably the CDS seller for some synthetic CDO that Merrill bought for HNW clients.  

From a bberg article at the time:

“…Buyers of credit-default swaps tied to Harrah's, the world's biggest casino-operator by sales, made as much as 40 percent in the two weeks ending Sept. 29 as the contracts based on $10 million of bonds jumped to $112,000 from $80,000, according to data compiled by Credit Suisse. The Las Vegas-based company said on Oct. 2 it received a leveraged-buyout offer from Apollo in New York and Dallas-based Texas Pacific, pushing the price of the credit derivatives to a record $250,000.”

text:
This is truly a case of a thoughtless, factless, emotionally driven example of anecdotal opinion, dressed up as factual reporting.  Responding logically to this mess is truly challenging because the post is devoid of all logic.  So, let's talk about Ken Paxton. shall we?

The hung jury and the child’s understandable reluctance to endure another trial are context—not absolution. Paxton’s office still offered misdemeanor pleas and effectively one day in jail. The judge rejected that sentence and imposed 60 days; Hoffman served 29. The question isn’t whether a retrial would have been difficult. It’s whether that original offer was remotely proportionate.

And Paxton’s air of entitlement is hard to miss. Eight senior officials in his own office reported him to the FBI over suspected abuses of office. A Republican-controlled Texas House impeached him 121–23; Naturally, the Texas Senate later acquitted him. 

Securities regulators found that he violated registration law and fined him. He later paid $271,000 in restitution under a diversion agreement that ended felony securities charges without a conviction. More recently, reporters found apparent omissions involving rental income and roughly $1.3 million in mortgages in his financial disclosures. Those aren’t all criminal convictions—but they are part of the documented record.

Let's further talk about the man who lectures everyone else on election integrity? Paxton voted in six elections while registered at a Collin County home his wife said he’d moved out of in 2024. Reporters linked him to a home in another county, and a formal complaint requested an investigation. Fraud hasn’t been established, but the discrepancy deserves an answer—not another lecture.

Then, instead of defending the plea offer, you pivot to “thousands of kids” supposedly harmed by Talarico’s “trans kids policies.” Which policy? Which children? What evidence? Talarico’s positions are fair game for a separate debate. But an unsupported claim about other children does nothing to explain this plea offer. THE RIGHT’S TOP 10  🦅

Daily News Report — September 28, 2026

Edition compiled  08:00 p.m. ET

"To be persuasive we must be believable; to be believable we must be credible; to be credible we must be truthful." — Edward R. Murrow

Purpose. This briefing organizes the day’s most consequential national headlines as they were reported and framed by leading conservative and center-right outlets. It is a synthesis, not original reporting. Claims are presented as they appeared in that coverage and, where useful, noted against same-day wire accounts so the reader can separate confirmed developments from political argument.

Source pool: major conservative-leaning and center-right outlets, including Fox News/Fox Business, Wall Street Journal, New York Post, Newsmax, Daily Wire, Breitbart, Washington Examiner, Washington Times, Just the News, National Review, and similar publications. I prioritized stories that appeared across multiple qualifying outlets or were especially prominent within the source pool. Opinion pieces and partisan commentary were generally excluded from the factual summaries.

Below is a September 28-only roundup drawn from the requested conservative and center-right source pool. I prioritized stories appearing prominently across multiple outlets where possible and excluded opinion pieces from the factual roundup.

Foreign Policy And Armed Conflict 🌍

🇮🇷 U.S.-Iran diplomacy remains stalled amid pressure over nuclear concessions

The Wall Street Journal reported that mediators are pressing Iran to accept nuclear-related concessions in an effort to revive negotiations with Washington. The effort comes amid continuing tensions over the Strait of Hormuz and after President Trump rejected a proposed seven-day truce.

The Washington Times likewise reported that Iranian officials were meeting with mediators in New York over proposals concerning the conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

🇬🇧 UK terror-plot arrests put Iran under scrutiny

Fox News reported that British counterterrorism authorities arrested five suspects near RAF Fairford, a military base used by the U.S., in an alleged plot involving explosives. The report said authorities were investigating possible links to Iran.

The Washington Times and Breitbart reported separately that the five suspects were subsequently released on bail, generating criticism from President Trump over the British decision.

🇮🇱 Egypt's warning before Oct. 7 draws renewed scrutiny

The Wall Street Journal reported that Egypt's intelligence chief warned Israeli officials about an impending Hamas attack before the October 7, 2023 assault. Newsmax also reported on the warning, saying the Egyptian official made an unannounced trip to Israel 11 days before the attack.

🇨🇳 U.S.-China tensions remain part of the foreign-policy agenda

The Washington Times reported that Trump denied discussing an offer to sell U.S. weapons to China during his recent summit with President Xi Jinping. Fox News' Monday coverage also highlighted the conclusion of the Trump-Xi state visit and continuing differences between Washington and Beijing.

Government Dysfunction • Poor Leadership • Political Division • Corruption 🤡

🏛️ Senate remains in Washington amid fight over AI data-center electricity costs

Fox News reported that Senate Republicans are keeping senators in Washington for a vote concerning electricity costs associated with large AI data centers. The dispute has become intertwined with the 2026 midterm campaign, with Democrats and Republicans disagreeing over whether the legislation sufficiently protects utility customers from potentially higher costs.

💰 Trump administration faces criticism over taxpayer-funded advertising

The Washington Examiner reported that the administration spent approximately $316,000 on advertising during NFL and college-football broadcasts between September 25 and 27. Sen. John Thune criticized the use of taxpayer funds for what he characterized as campaign-style public-service advertising while saying he supported the underlying message.

🏛️ FBI leadership change

Fox News reported that FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey announced his resignation after roughly a year in the position, citing family reasons and a desire to return to Missouri.

⚖️ Missouri redistricting dispute remains an election-administration problem

Missouri's congressional-map fight continues to generate conflicting court orders. Fox News reported that the Supreme Court had ordered the state to use its 2022 map for the November election, while an earlier appeals-court ruling had required the newer map after Missouri conducted its August primary under those districts. The dispute illustrates the administrative difficulties created by changing congressional boundaries between a primary and general election.

Immigration And The Border 🛂

🇺🇸 Immigration enforcement remains politically contentious

Fox News reported that the Trump administration recently denied reports that ICE had instructed agents to limit arrests primarily to immigrants with criminal records. The administration said there had been no change in enforcement policy, while reporting described internal confusion over guidance emphasizing the highest-priority offenders.

🇪🇸 Migrant protests in Spain highlight continuing European border pressures

Breitbart reported that more than 1,000 residents of Ceuta participated in a sit-in near the Moroccan border, demanding action over continuing migration pressures in the Spanish North African enclave.

🇺🇸 H-1B visas become part of the immigration/workforce debate

Fox News reported that Vice President JD Vance is advocating changes to the H-1B system, arguing that some technology companies use foreign-worker visas in ways that displace American workers. His comments place legal immigration and skilled-worker visas alongside illegal immigration in the administration's broader immigration debate.

Crime • Violence • Gun Violence • Drug Addiction 💀

🔫 New York Times Games executive killed in California

Fox News reported that Jonathan McKinsey, a 40-year-old New York Times Games engineering director, was fatally shot in Dublin, California. Police arrested his 77-year-old parents-in-law at the scene on suspicion of murder; authorities had not announced a motive as of the report.

🚲 Central Park death highlights violent incidents in New York

The New York Post reported that a father of two was killed after being struck by a bicyclist while walking through Central Park on his way to work.

National Unity • Polarization • State Of Democracy 🗳️

🗺️ Missouri's congressional-map fight underscores election-system uncertainty

The Missouri redistricting litigation continued to generate competing interpretations of which congressional boundaries should govern the November election. Fox News reported that more than 1.2 million Missourians had already voted in the August primary under the newer map, while subsequent court action affected which map could be used for November.

The dispute has prompted competing arguments from election officials, lawyers, and voting-rights advocates over the constitutional and administrative consequences of changing district boundaries after a primary.

🗳️ Midterm politics increasingly centers on affordability

Fox News reported that affordability and economic conditions are becoming major issues in the approaching midterm elections, with polling indicating substantial voter dissatisfaction with inflation and the cost of living.

Health Costs, Energy, And The Cost Of Living 💸

⛽ Oil and diesel prices remain a major economic concern

Fox Business reported September 28 that crude oil had reached approximately $94 per barrel, while the national average diesel price was reported at roughly $6.45 per gallon. The report also highlighted a 10-year Treasury yield above 5.2% and uncertainty surrounding the Middle East conflict.

Newsmax separately reported that U.S. stocks fell Monday as higher oil prices and Treasury yields weighed on markets, with investors watching developments surrounding the Iran conflict.

⚡ AI data centers and utility bills become a political issue

The Senate dispute over AI data-center electricity requirements is also directly tied to household energy costs. Republicans and Democrats are debating whether rapidly expanding data-center demand could shift infrastructure costs onto ordinary utility customers.

Economy • Federal Budget Deficit • National Debt 📉

🏭 Trump announces $15 billion Iowa steel project

Trump announced plans for a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa, described by the Washington Times and New York Post as a major test of the administration's tariff-driven industrial policy. The administration is presenting the project as evidence of increased domestic manufacturing investment.

📈 Stocks decline as oil and Treasury yields rise

Newsmax reported that U.S. stocks fell Monday as higher oil prices and Treasury yields increased pressure on markets. Investors were weighing both Middle East risks and uncertainty surrounding the broader economic outlook.

💵 Federal debt and interest costs remain enormous

The Washington Examiner reported that federal debt surpassed $40 trillion in August and cited Congressional Budget Office projections for a fiscal-year 2026 deficit of approximately $2.1 trillion. Its report also highlighted the rapidly increasing cost of servicing the debt.

Note: the Examiner article is an opinion piece, so the figures above are presented as reported figures rather than as an independent assessment of the fiscal outlook.

Poverty • Homelessness • Related Social Issues 🏚️

🏙️ Homeless Central Park artist identified after fatal attack

The New York Post reported that a homeless artist known for painting Central Park's birds was identified as the woman found beaten to death in a park gazebo. The case drew attention both because of the killing and because of the victim's life as a well-known figure among people living in and around the park.

🏙️ Boston immigrant-services program draws dispute over eligibility

Fox News reported that Boston Mayor Michelle Wu's administration is funding a civic-engagement scholarship program restricted to immigrants, including non-U.S. citizens. Critics argued that the eligibility requirements exclude citizens, while the administration's program is framed around civic engagement among immigrant communities.

OVERALL DAILY SUMMARY 📝

September 28's conservative and center-right coverage was dominated by three interconnected themes: foreign-policy tensions, domestic political conflict, and economic affordability.

The Iran conflict and attempted diplomacy remained the most significant international story, with negotiations over Iran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz occurring alongside reports of an alleged terror plot near a U.S.-used British air base. The Egyptian warning about the 2023 Hamas attack also generated renewed scrutiny of what Israeli and Egyptian officials knew before October 7.

Domestically, government and electoral disputes remained prominent. The Missouri congressional-map litigation continued to raise questions about election administration after voters had already participated in a primary under one set of districts. At the federal level, Senate Republicans remained in Washington over legislation concerning AI data-center electricity costs, while controversy continued over taxpayer-funded administration advertising.

The economy and affordability were another major thread. A $15 billion Iowa steel project was presented by the administration as evidence of domestic industrial investment, while higher oil, diesel and Treasury yields were weighing on markets and household-cost concerns remained prominent in political coverage.

Finally, crime, immigration and social disorder remained substantial components of the day's coverage, ranging from the California shooting and Central Park homicide to continuing disputes over immigration enforcement and European migration pressures.

Bottom line: The September 28 coverage presents a news environment in which war and diplomacy abroad, election and institutional disputes at home, and persistent concerns about prices, energy, immigration and public safety were the dominant recurring subjects across the selected conservative and center-right outlets.

text:
Trump called Ravid's Axios story a hoax and demanded it be withdrawn "IMMEDIATELY." What he didn't do is deny the substance: that mediators are in New York today meeting Iran's foreign minister on a Qatari proposal, that indirect talks are underway, or that a US official is on record calling the negotiations "positive and constructive." His denial is narrowly about the word "offered" and the framing of sanctions relief, not the diplomatic process itself, which Axios sourced to multiple US officials and which Trump's own post doesn't contest.

This is the same denial pattern we flagged with the Israel-UAE warning story weeks ago, and with the wedding-gift payment claim before that: Trump's public denial and his own officials' on-record statements point in different directions. Here the gap is unusually narrow and precise. "I offered them NOTHING" is compatible with a US official simultaneously telling Axios that Iran "has indicated they are flexible on the nuclear issues" and that the administration wants "assurances" before finalizing anything, language that describes an active negotiation over exactly the kind of concessions Trump says he never offered.

The substantive tension in the reporting matters more than the Truth Social post. Iran wants the talks centered on Hormuz and the naval blockade, the same chokepoint fight we've tracked for weeks through disputed traffic numbers and dueling tanker counts. The US is holding the line on nuclear concessions first. A US official's own framing, "the U.S. position gets stronger every day," while insisting Washington "remains patient," reads as leverage rhetoric for a negotiation still very much in progress, not the posture of an administration that offered nothing and has nothing on the table.

The credibility question this raises is really about the last MOU, which the same official cites as the reason for present-day skepticism: Iran allegedly fired on commercial vessels in Hormuz in July, breaking that agreement within weeks of signing it. If that history is the actual obstacle, "no offer exists" is a strange thing to insist on while your own officials are describing exactly what terms are being negotiated and why trust, not substance, is the sticking point.

text:
⚡️🇺🇸🇨🇳🇹🇼 — US Ambassador to China David Perdue said on Monday that President Donald Trump asked Chinese President Xi Jinping whether he wanted to buy US weapons, telling Fox News that Trump often notes Washington sells arms worldwide and «at some point he even asked President Xi if he wanted to buy some». 

The administration subsequently downplayed the remark: one US official said there are no plans to sell weapons to China, another said such sales are already prohibited by law and that Beijing had received neither proposals nor plans for such a deal, while Perdue did not clarify what he meant and White House and State Department spokespeople declined to say whether Trump raised the issue with Xi during their meeting the previous week or an earlier meeting — WSJ. 

➡️ The statement came after the Trump-Xi summit, where the two pledged continued communication and cooperation to avoid confrontation, amid debate over an additional $14 billion security package for Taiwan; four Republican senators had urged Trump to advance it, warning that US regional deterrence could be weakened if partners lacked essential defensive capabilities, while Financial Times reporting raised the possibility that the delay was intended to avoid friction with Xi. 

Perdue rejected claims that Trump is doing too little for Taiwan, saying the president had approved arms sales to the island at a level more than 50% higher than under any previous US president, and reaffirmed: «We do not support independence, and we do not support coercion». Washington had announced more than $11 billion in Taiwan arms deals in December, including artillery, missile launchers and UAVs, prompting anger in Beijing.

➡️ Experts cited in the reporting warned that Perdue’s remarks could raise doubts in Taiwan about US commitment, portraying China as a potential US arms customer in Trump’s view and potentially signaling an extraordinary policy shift if they reflected a genuine offer rather than a slip of the tongue. The accounts therefore leave a clear discrepancy between Perdue’s description and administration officials’ denial that any such offer was made, with no indication of an actual policy change.
